restrictions.note: No prescribing restrictions stated in the UK SmPC.

items.t: One 1.5 mg tablet every 24 hours, preferably in the morning. Higher doses do not add antihypertensive effect but increase the saluretic (diuretic) effect; do not increase the dose if treatment is ineffective.

src.q: One tablet per 24 hours, preferably in the morning
At higher doses the antihypertensive action of indapamide is not enhanced but the saluretic effect is increased.
The dose should not be increased if treatment is ineffective.

items.t: Elderly: can be treated when renal function is normal or only minimally impaired; interpret plasma creatinine in relation to age, weight and gender.

src.q: Elderly patients can be treated with Natrilix SR when renal function is normal or only minimally impaired.
In the elderly, the plasma creatinine must be adjusted in relation to age, weight and gender.

items.t: Safety and efficacy in children and adolescents have not been established; no data are available.

src.q: The safety and efficacy of Natrilix SR in children and adolescents have not been established. No data are available.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to indapamide, to other sulfonamides or to any excipient; severe renal failure; hepatic encephalopathy or severe impairment of liver function; hypokalaemia.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to the active substance, to other sulfonamides or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.
- Severe renal failure. - Hepatic encephalopathy or severe impairment of liver function. - Hypokalaemia.

items.t: Severe renal failure is defined in section 4.2 as creatinine clearance below 30 ml/min.

src.q: In severe renal failure (creatinine clearance below 30 ml/min), treatment is contraindicated.

items.t: Impaired liver function: thiazide-related diuretics may cause hepatic encephalopathy (especially with electrolyte imbalance), which can progress to hepatic coma. Stop immediately if this occurs.

src.q: When liver function is impaired, thiazide-related diuretics may cause, particularly in case of electrolyte imbalance, hepatic encephalopathy which can progress to hepatic coma.
Administration of the diuretic must be stopped immediately if this occurs.

items.t: Hyponatraemia (sometimes with very serious consequences): measure sodium before starting and regularly after; more often in the elderly and in cirrhosis.

src.q: This must be measured before starting treatment, then at regular intervals subsequently.
Any diuretic treatment may cause hyponatraemia, sometimes with very serious consequences.

items.t: Hypokalaemia is the major risk: prevent potassium below 3.4 mmol/l in high-risk groups (elderly, malnourished or on many medicines, cirrhosis with oedema/ascites, coronary disease, heart failure, long QT). Hypokalaemia and bradycardia predispose to torsades de pointes.

src.q: Potassium depletion with hypokalaemia is the major risk of thiazide and related diuretics.
The risk of onset of hypokalaemia (< 3.4 mmol/l) must be prevented in certain high risk populations
Individuals with a long QT interval are also at risk, whether the origin is congenital or iatrogenic.

items.t: Calcium may rise slightly; marked hypercalcaemia may reveal hyperparathyroidism (stop before testing parathyroid function). Hypomagnesaemia can occur.

src.q: Frank hypercalcaemia may be due to previously unrecognised hyperparathyroidism.
Treatment should be withdrawn before the investigation of parathyroid function.
which may result in hypomagnesaemia

items.t: Diabetes: monitoring of blood glucose is important, especially with hypokalaemia. Gout: attacks may be more likely in hyperuricaemia.

src.q: Monitoring of blood glucose is important in diabetics, in particular in the presence of hypokalaemia.
Tendency to gout attacks may be increased in hyperuricaemic patients.

items.t: Choroidal effusion, acute myopia and secondary acute angle-closure glaucoma can occur within hours to weeks; stop the drug as rapidly as possible. History of sulfonamide or penicillin allergy may be a risk factor.

src.q: The primary treatment is to discontinue drug intake as rapidly as possible.
Risk factors for developing acute angle-closure glaucoma may include a history of sulfonamide or penicillin allergy.

items.t: Photosensitivity: stop treatment if it occurs; if re-treatment is needed, protect skin from sun and artificial UVA.

src.q: If photosensitivity reaction occurs during treatment, it is recommended to stop the treatment.
it is recommended to protect exposed areas to the sun or to artificial UVA

items.t: Lactose: patients with galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.

src.q: Patients with rare hereditary problems of galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.

items.t: Sulfonamide allergy (SPS): cross-reactivity between sulfonamide antibiotics and non-antibiotic sulfonamides (which include thiazides and thiazide-like diuretics) is not expected, but product information often contraindicates them. This SmPC lists hypersensitivity to other sulfonamides as a contraindication.

src.q: thiazides and thiazide-like diuretics
Cross-reactivity between antibiotic and non-antibiotic sulfonamides is not expected, including in people who had a life-threatening reaction to a sulfonamide.

items.t: Lithium: combination not recommended (raised lithium, toxicity). If a diuretic is needed, monitor plasma lithium carefully and adjust the dose.

src.q: Combinations that are not recommended: Lithium: Increased plasma lithium with signs of overdosage
careful monitoring of plasma lithium and dose adjustment are required.

items.t: Medicines that can cause torsades de pointes (e.g. class Ia and III antiarrhythmics, some antipsychotics, moxifloxacin, methadone): higher risk of ventricular arrhythmia, as hypokalaemia is a risk factor. Correct hypokalaemia first; monitor clinically, electrolytes and ECG.

src.q: Increased risk of ventricular arrhythmias, particularly torsades de pointes (hypokalaemia is a risk factor).
Monitor for hypokalaemia and correct, if required, before introducing this combination. Clinical, plasma electrolytes and ECG monitoring.

items.t: NSAIDs (systemic, including COX-2 inhibitors) and high-dose aspirin (3 g/day or more): may reduce the antihypertensive effect; risk of acute renal failure if dehydrated. Hydrate the patient and monitor renal function at the start.

src.q: N.S.A.I.Ds. (systemic route) including COX-2 selective inhibitors, high dose acetylsalicylic acid (≥ 3 g/day)
Risk of acute renal failure in dehydrated patients (decreased glomerular filtration). Hydrate the patient; monitor renal function at the start of treatment.

items.t: ACE inhibitors: risk of sudden hypotension and/or acute renal failure when started with pre-existing sodium depletion. Either stop the diuretic 3 days before, or start the ACE inhibitor at a low dose; monitor creatinine in the first weeks.

src.q: Risk of sudden hypotension and/or acute renal failure
either to stop the diuretic 3 days before starting treatment with the A.C.E. inhibitor
monitor renal function (plasma creatinine) during the first weeks of treatment

items.t: Other potassium-lowering medicines (systemic corticosteroids, stimulant laxatives, IV amphotericin B, tetracosactide): additive hypokalaemia; monitor and correct potassium; use non-stimulant laxatives. Systemic corticosteroids also reduce the antihypertensive effect.

src.q: gluco- and mineralo-corticoids (systemic route), tetracosactide, stimulant laxatives: Increased risk of hypokalaemia (additive effect).
Use non-stimulant laxatives.
Decreased antihypertensive effect (water/sodium retention due to corticosteroids).

items.t: Potassium-sparing diuretics (amiloride, spironolactone): hypokalaemia or hyperkalaemia can still occur, especially in renal failure or diabetes; monitor potassium and ECG.

src.q: hypokalaemia or hyperkalaemia (particularly in patients with renal failure or diabetes) may still occur. Plasma potassium and ECG should be monitored

items.t: Metformin: higher risk of lactic acidosis from diuretic-related renal impairment. Do not use metformin when plasma creatinine exceeds 135 µmol/l (men) or 110 µmol/l (women).

src.q: Increased risk of metformin induced lactic acidosis
Do not use metformin when plasma creatinine exceeds 15 mg/l (135 µmol/l) in men and 12 mg/l (110 µmol/l) in women.

items.t: Allopurinol: more hypersensitivity reactions to allopurinol. Tricyclic (imipramine-like) antidepressants and neuroleptics: additive orthostatic hypotension. Calcium salts: risk of hypercalcaemia. Digitalis: hypokalaemia/hypomagnesaemia increase toxicity (monitor potassium, magnesium and ECG). Iodinated contrast: rehydrate first. Baclofen: increased antihypertensive effect. Ciclosporin, tacrolimus: plasma creatinine may rise.

src.q: Concomitant treatment with indapamide may increase the incidence of hypersensitivity reactions to allopurinol.
Imipramine-like antidepressants, neuroleptics: Antihypertensive effect and increased risk of orthostatic hypotension (additive effect).
Calcium (salts): Risk of hypercalcaemia resulting from decreased urinary elimination of calcium.
Hypokalaemia and/or hypomagnesaemia predispose to the toxic effects of digitalis.
Rehydration before administration of the iodinated compound.
Baclofen: Increased antihypertensive effect.
Ciclosporin, tacrolimus: Risk of increased plasma creatinine

items.t: Contraindicated in severe renal failure (creatinine clearance below 30 ml/min). Thiazide-related diuretics are fully effective only when renal function is normal or minimally impaired (plasma creatinine below about 220 µmol/l in an adult).

src.q: In severe renal failure (creatinine clearance below 30 ml/min), treatment is contraindicated.
plasma creatinine below levels of the order of 25 mg/l, i.e . 220 µmol/l in an adult

items.t: Early hypovolaemia can reduce glomerular filtration and worsen existing renal insufficiency.

src.q: This transitory functional renal insufficiency is of no consequence in individuals with normal renal function but may worsen preexisting renal insufficiency.

items.t: Contraindicated in severe hepatic impairment or hepatic encephalopathy. In any liver impairment, risk of hepatic encephalopathy; stop immediately if it occurs.

src.q: In severe hepatic impairment, treatment is contraindicated.
Hepatic encephalopathy or severe impairment of liver function.

items.t: SmPC: limited data. Prolonged third-trimester thiazide exposure can reduce maternal plasma volume and uteroplacental blood flow (fetoplacental ischaemia, growth retardation). Preferably avoid in pregnancy as a precaution.

src.q: Prolonged exposure to thiazide during the third trimester of pregnancy can reduce maternal plasma volume as well as uteroplacental blood flow
As a precautionary measure, it is preferable to avoid the use of Indapamide during pregnancy.

items.t: BUMPS (diuretics): can be used in pregnancy if prescribed by a doctor but rarely needed; may reduce blood flow to the placenta, so extra growth scans are offered. For hypertension a different medicine is usually offered.

src.q: A diuretic can be used in pregnancy if prescribed by a doctor.
Diuretics may reduce blood flow to the placenta.
If you take a diuretic to treat high blood pressure, you will usually be offered a different medicine that is known to be safe during pregnancy.

items.t: Not recommended. Insufficient information on excretion in milk; risk of sulfonamide hypersensitivity and hypokalaemia in the infant cannot be excluded; thiazides can reduce or suppress milk production.

src.q: Indapamide is not recommended during breast-feeding.
A risk to the newborns/infants cannot be excluded.
decrease or even suppression of milk lactation

items.t: No effect on fertility in rat studies; no effects on human fertility are anticipated.

src.q: No effects on human fertility are anticipated.

items.t: Common: hypokalaemia, hypersensitivity reactions (mainly skin, in people prone to allergy/asthma), maculopapular rash. At 1.5 mg, potassium below 3.4 mmol/l was seen in 10% of patients after 4-6 weeks.

src.q: The most commonly reported adverse reactions are hypokalaemia, hypersensitivity reactions, mainly dermatological, in subjects with a predisposition to allergic and asthmatic reactions and maculopapular rashes.

src.q: Symptoms include acute onset of decreased visual acuity or ocular pain and typically occur within hours to weeks of drug initiation.

items.t: Very rare: agranulocytosis, aplastic or haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, angioedema, toxic epidermal necrolysis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, pancreatitis, renal failure. Hepatic encephalopathy possible in liver failure.
